system: Chinese shichen (十二時辰) — the twelve earthly-branch double-hours, as a FIXED CIVIL division of the whole nychthemeron, with the 刻 (ke) subdivision layer (100-ke before 1645, 96-ke after) and the almanac (通勝 / 通書) auspicious-hour layer laid over it
compiledFor: Horae Mundi — comparative temporal rulership. Data dossier only; no code, no assets touched.
dayStart: The shichen day begins at the START of 子時 (zǐ shí), i.e. at civil-clock 23:00 of the preceding Gregorian date, and the twelve divisions then run 23:00→01:00→03:00→… . This is the mainstream convention and the one the modern almanac and modern bazi practice use (子時換日). The anchor is NOT sunrise, NOT sunset and NOT any solar event: it is the midnight point, and 子 is named 夜半 ('mid-night') because it STRADDLES midnight rather than beginning at it. TWO ATTESTED DEPARTURES, both kept: (i) Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004) find that in the Song dynasty the first double-hour BEGAN at 0h local time, so 子 = 00:00–02:00 and every division shifts one hour later [src: soma-2004, en-wiki-tct]; (ii) a modern minority of bazi practitioners, following 袁樹珊 (Yuan Shushan), change the DAY at 子正 (00:00) rather than at 子初 (23:00), so a birth at 23:30 keeps the current day's stem-branch — the 早子時/晚子時 (or 夜子時) dispute [src: lnka-zaozi, tier C]. The three positions are not reconciled here.
divisionRule: ONE nychthemeron (晝夜, a full day-and-night) is divided into TWELVE EQUAL parts, each named for one of the twelve earthly branches (地支) in fixed order 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥. Each part is therefore exactly 1/12 of 24 hours = 2 hours of constant length, every day of the year, at every latitude. THE DIVISION IS OF THE WHOLE DAY, NOT OF DAYLIGHT. This is the structural point on which shichen differ from Greco-Roman planetary hours and from any seasonal-hour scheme: there is no separate count of day-hours and night-hours, no expansion in summer and contraction in winter, and no dependence on sunrise or sunset. The primary evidence is arithmetical and explicit: 隋書·天文志上 records that in Liang 天監 6 (507 CE) Emperor Wu found that '晝夜百刻，分配十二辰，辰得八刻，仍有餘分' — the hundred ke of the day-and-night, distributed over the twelve chen, give each chen eight ke with a remainder left over — and so reformed the day to 96 ke 'so that one chen has eight whole ke' (一辰有全刻八焉). A scheme that distributes a FIXED total (100 ke, then 96 ke) evenly over twelve chen is by construction a scheme of equal fixed divisions of the whole day [src: suishu-19]. The seasonal variation in the same source sits in a DIFFERENT place — in how the fixed ke are split between daylight and darkness ('冬至晝漏四十刻，夜漏六十刻。夏至晝漏六十刻，夜漏四十刻。春秋二分，晝夜各五十刻') — and in the 更 (gēng) night-watch layer, which IS variable. The chen themselves do not move. SUBDIVISION: each shichen is halved into 初 (chū, 'initial') and 正 (zhèng, 'central'), a practice the sources place from the late Tang into the Song, giving 24 half-shichen that align one-to-one with the 24 Western hours [src: en-wiki-tct, zh-wiki-shichen]. Below that sits the ke: under the 100-ke system a shichen is 8⅓ ke (each half-shichen 4⅙ ke, i.e. 4 大刻 plus a 小刻 of ⅙); under the 96-ke system a shichen is exactly 8 ke of 15 minutes, named 初初刻・初一刻・初二刻・初三刻・正初刻・正一刻・正二刻・正三刻, with 正初刻 also written 初四刻 and the NEXT shichen's 初初刻 also written 正四刻 [src: zh-wiki-ke, lin-2007].

structuralContrast.vsPlanetaryHours: The repo's assets/js/core/planetary-hours.js divides sunrise→sunset into 12 and sunset→sunrise into 12, so hour length varies with season and latitude and the day begins at sunrise. Shichen do NONE of that: 12 equal parts of one 24-hour span, day begins at 23:00 civil. A comparison view must not reuse the seasonal-hour machinery for shichen.
structuralContrast.vsMuhurta: The repo's assets/js/core/muhurta.js divides sunrise→sunset (and the night) into 15 muhūrtas plus octant kālas, all sunrise-anchored and therefore seasonal and latitude-sensitive. Shichen share neither the anchor nor the variability.
structuralContrast.whatIsSeasonalInThisSystem: Only two layers: (a) the daylight/darkness SPLIT of the fixed ke total (冬至 40/60, 夏至 60/40, equinoxes 50/50 per 隋書); and (b) the five 更 night-watches, which run dusk→dawn and are therefore variable — en-wiki-tct records Western-Han and post-102-CE schemes for adjusting the start of 一更 through the year. Neither touches the twelve chen.

entries.name: zi
entries.ruler: unattested — the shichen carries NO fixed ruler. Rulership in this system is not a property of the hour; it is assigned per-day by the almanac layer, as a function of the DAY's earthly branch (see variants.tongshu-huangdao and goldenValues gv-3/gv-4).
entries.quality: 夜半 yèbàn, 'mid-night' — the division straddles midnight rather than beginning at it
entries.note: The name 夜半 is the reason the mainstream boundary is 23:00–01:00 and not 00:00–02:00: the hour is centred on midnight. Sôma et al. (2004) nonetheless find the Song dynasty began the first chen AT 0h. Both are recorded; neither is resolved here.

entries.note: A REAL FINDING, and the most interesting cell in the table: 辰 is the ONE branch 論衡 物勢篇 does not give an animal. That chapter supplies eleven of the twelve (子鼠 丑牛 寅虎 卯兔 巳蛇 午馬 未羊 申猴 酉雞 戌犬 亥豕) and is silent on 辰. The dragon comes from a DIFFERENT chapter of the same work, 言毒篇: '辰為龍，巳為蛇，辰巳之位在東南'. So the earliest complete twelve-animal set in 論衡 is a reconstruction across two chapters, not a single list.

keSystemHistory.summary: The ke (刻) is the subdivision layer beneath the shichen, and it is the layer that actually moved. The shichen count never changed; the ke count changed at least five times.

events.label: The 100-ke baseline
events.when: The standard through most of recorded practice; en-wiki-tct puts it as the usual definition 'until 1628'
events.value: 1 day = 100 ke; 1 ke = 14.4 min = 14 min 24 s; 1 shichen = 8⅓ ke
events.verbatim: 其法，總以百刻，分於晝夜。冬至晝漏四十刻，夜漏六十刻。夏至晝漏六十刻，夜漏四十刻。春秋二分，晝夜各五十刻。
events.note: The 40/60 solstice split is a schematic figure. 60 ke × 14.4 min = 14.4 h of daylight at midsummer. 隋書 states no latitude for it. Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004) independently find that Chinese daytime-length, sunrise/sunset and gnomon-shadow tables correspond to a standard latitude of about 34.5°N — I have NOT verified that the 40/60 figure is the datum they are describing, and no cited scholar is here connecting the two.

events.label: 120 ke under Wang Mang's Xin
events.when: Han period; reported as a Han-era modification
events.note: UNVERIFIED AGAINST A PRIMARY LOCUS. en-wiki-tct records that days of 96, 108 or 120 ke existed for short periods before 1628 but gives no dates; the Wang Mang attribution reached me only through tertiary sources. See gaps.

events.label: FIRST 96-ke reform — Liang, 天監 6 (507 CE)
events.verbatim: 至天監六年，武帝以晝夜百刻，分配十二辰，辰得八刻，仍有餘分。乃以晝夜為九十六刻，一辰有全刻八焉。
events.note: THIS MATTERS FOR THE HEADLINE CLAIM. The 96-ke idea is not a Jesuit import: it was tried in 507 CE, eleven centuries early, and for exactly the same arithmetical reason — 100 does not divide by 12. Any page that presents 96 ke as a European contribution is wrong, and the 隋書 sentence is the proof.

events.label: 108 ke — Liang, 大同 10 (544 CE)
events.verbatim: 至大同十年，又改用一百八刻。依《尚書考靈曜》晝夜三十六頃之數，因而三之。
events.note: Justified from the apocryphal 尚書考靈曜's 36 qǐng of day-and-night, tripled.

events.label: Reversion to 100 ke — Chen, 天嘉 era (560–566 CE)
events.when: 天嘉 era of Chen Wendi
events.verbatim: 陳文帝天嘉中，亦命舍人硃史造漏，依古百刻為法。

events.label: THE 96-ke REFORM THAT STUCK — 時憲曆, Shunzhi 2 (1645)
events.when: 1645 (順治二年), with the 崇禎曆書 groundwork from the late Ming (c. 1628–1634)
events.value: 1 day = 96 ke; 1 ke = 15 min exactly; 1 shichen = 8 ke; 1 Western hour = 4 ke
events.note: This is the reform the brief asks about, and the clean '1645' story is NOT clean. See keSystemHistory.reformContested.

reformContested.claim: The 96-ke system was adopted in 1645 with the 時憲曆 and that was that.
reformContested.whyItIsTooTidy: 清史稿·時憲志 records the reform being litigated at court for a quarter-century afterwards. Under Shunzhi the Jesuit Johann Adam Schall von Bell (湯若望) carried the new calendar. Then, in the Kangxi Calendar Case (康熙曆獄), Yang Guangxian (楊光先) had Schall condemned and Ferdinand Verbiest (南懷仁) exiled; the older methods were restored under Wu Mingxuan. 清史稿 卷45 preserves the ke question as a live item of that dispute — '康熙四年，議政王等言：每日百刻，新法改為九十六刻' (Kangxi 4 = 1665) — and then the vindication after the observatory trial: '圖海等赴觀象台測驗，南懷仁所言皆合…竊思百刻雖行之已久，但南懷仁九十六刻之法既合天象，自應頒用.' Tertiary accounts of the case report Yang Guangxian arguing that China's calendar uses 100 ke while the Western one uses 96, and that adopting the Western reckoning would shorten the dynasty's fortune — I have that argument at Tier C only and have not verified its wording in a primary source.

positions.position: Still contested at court in Kangxi 4 (1665) and only settled after the Verbiest observatory trial of Kangxi 7–8 (1668–69)

reformContested.resolution: NOT RESOLVED HERE. Both are printed. An engine that offers a 'pre-reform / post-reform' toggle should not label the boundary a single year without saying whose account that year comes from.
reformContested.furtherCaution: en-wiki-tct dates the definition change to 1628 (the 崇禎曆書 project) rather than 1645 (promulgation). A third position, and also printed.

variants.label: 子 = 23:00–01:00 (mainstream)
variants.authority: Mainstream in every source consulted, classical and modern; the branch's own name 夜半 ('mid-night') presupposes it
variants.arithmetic: shichenIndex = floor(((civilHour + 1) mod 24) / 2); boundaries at odd hours 23,01,03,…,21

variants.label: 子 = 00:00–02:00 (Song dynasty)
variants.authority: Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004), PASJ 56(5):887–904 — 'the first double hour began at 0 hr local time' in the Song; carried as a separate column in en-wiki-tct
variants.arithmetic: shichenIndex = floor(civilHour / 2); boundaries at even hours 00,02,04,…,22

variants.label: 100-ke subdivision (pre-1645)
variants.authority: 隋書·天文志上 for the arithmetic; the standard before the Qing reform
variants.arithmetic: 1 ke = 1/100 day = 14.4 min. 1 shichen = 8⅓ ke; each half-shichen = 4⅙ ke, i.e. four 大刻 plus one 小刻 of ⅙ ke. Ke boundaries therefore do NOT align with shichen boundaries and drift through the day.

variants.label: 96-ke subdivision (1645 onward)
variants.arithmetic: 1 ke = 1/96 day = 15 min exactly. 1 shichen = 8 ke, named 初初刻・初一刻・初二刻・初三刻・正初刻・正一刻・正二刻・正三刻. 正初刻 is alternately written 初四刻; the NEXT shichen's 初初刻 is alternately written 正四刻. Below the ke, 新法算書 divides 1 刻 = 100 分 and 1 分 = 100 秒 (decimal, not sexagesimal). Notation examples preserved: 未初初刻零八十三分 (a point 83 fen after 未初初刻), 酉初四刻內九十三分六十秒.

variants.label: The two ke-naming conventions are ALIASES, not rival boundaries
variants.authority: zh-wiki-ke, citing 新法算書 and the Qing 時憲書 practice
variants.arithmetic: Convention A (0-indexed within each half): 初初刻・初一刻・初二刻・初三刻 / 正初刻・正一刻・正二刻・正三刻. Convention B (1–4 within each half, as reported by en-wiki-tct: '子初一刻' through '子正四刻'): the same eight slots renumbered. The reconciling fact is that 正初刻 is also called 初四刻 and the next shichen's 初初刻 is also called 正四刻 — i.e. the two schemes name the same instants. This was initially recorded here as a possible unresolved conflict and was RESOLVED by zh-wiki-ke; the resolution is at Tier C and would benefit from a primary check against a printed 時憲書.

variants.label: 更 (gēng) — the FIVE night watches, which ARE variable
variants.authority: en-wiki-tct, citing 隋書 and Petersen (1992) on the 102 CE clepsydra reform
variants.arithmetic: Five watches 一更…五更 (初更 as an alternate for the first) spanning night. en-wiki-tct reports the first gēng theoretically at sundown but standardised to 酉正一刻 = 19:12, with the interval between gēng at 1/10 of a day = 2 h 24 min. Seasonal adjustment schemes are recorded: in the Western Han (206 BCE–102 CE) 一更 moved back one ke every 9th day from winter to summer solstice and forward again; from 102 CE the 四分曆 scheme added or subtracted a ke whenever the sun moved 2.5° in declination.
variants.note: THIS is where seasonality lives in Chinese timekeeping. Do not merge it into the shichen layer. A comparison engine that wants a seasonal Chinese hour has the gēng, not the chen.

variants.label: 五鼠遁 — deriving the hour's STEM from the day's stem
variants.authority: Practitioner mnemonic, universally reported and mutually consistent across the Tier C sources consulted; the standard attribution is to 淵海子平, which I could NOT verify (see gaps)
variants.arithmetic: The sixty-term stem-branch cycle runs continuously over double-hours, anchored so that the 子 hour of a 甲 or 己 day is 甲子. Mnemonic: 甲己還加甲，乙庚丙作初，丙辛從戊起，丁壬庚子居，戊癸何方發，壬子是真途 — i.e. the 子-hour stem is 甲 on 甲/己 days, 丙 on 乙/庚 days, 戊 on 丙/辛 days, 庚 on 丁/壬 days, 壬 on 戊/癸 days. Closed form: hourStemIndex = ((dayStemIndex mod 5) * 2 + branchIndex) mod 10, with 甲=0 and 子=0. NOTE: this layer needs the DAY's stem-branch, which this system does not itself supply — see gaps.day-ganzhi.

variants.label: ALMANAC LAYER — the 黃道 / 黑道 twelve spirits applied to the twelve hours
variants.authority: 欽定協紀辨方書 (1741, imperially commissioned, 允祿 et al.), 卷32 六十日時辰定局 — a printed 60-day × 12-hour table. THIS IS ALMANAC MATERIAL, NOT CANONICAL COSMOLOGY, and the brief's instruction to label it as such is honoured: nothing in 隋書, 論衡 or 五行大義 assigns rulership to a shichen.
variants.arithmetic: The twelve spirits run in the fixed order 青龍・明堂・天刑・朱雀・金匱・天德(printed 寶光 in the 四庫全書 text)・白虎・玉堂・天牢・玄武(printed 元武)・司命・勾陳. 青龍 is seated on an hour determined by the DAY's earthly branch, by the mnemonic 寅申須加子，卯酉卻在寅，辰戌龍位上，巳亥午上存，子午臨申地，丑未戌上行 — i.e. day-branch 寅/申 → 青龍 at 子時; 卯/酉 → 寅; 辰/戌 → 辰; 巳/亥 → 午; 子/午 → 申; 丑/未 → 戌. The remaining eleven follow in order round the twelve hours. Closed form: anchorBranch = (dayBranchIndex * 2 + 8) mod 12 with 子=0; spiritIndex(h) = (h − anchorBranch + 12) mod 12. SIX are 黃道 (auspicious): 青龍・明堂・金匱・天德/寶光・玉堂・司命 — indices 0,1,4,5,7,10. SIX are 黑道: 天刑・朱雀・白虎・天牢・玄武・勾陳 — indices 2,3,6,8,9,11.
variants.verification: The closed form was CHECKED against the printed 協紀辨方書 卷32 table and reproduces the 甲子日 and 乙丑日 rows cell-for-cell. See goldenValues gv-3 and gv-4.

variants.label: ALMANAC LAYER — 貴登天門時 and 四大吉時
variants.authority: 欽定協紀辨方書 卷32, two further sections after 六十日時辰定局
variants.arithmetic: 貴登天門時定局 ('the noble ascends the gate of heaven') is tabulated by SOLAR TERM (雨水後 through 大寒後) crossed with the day's heavenly stem, giving the hours at which the male/female 貴人 stars occupy the favoured palaces — so unlike the 黃道 layer it IS seasonally keyed. 四大吉時定局 tabulates four auspicious hour-types by season against the day stem, with associated officials 勾陳・六合・天乙・太常. NEITHER is transcribed in detail here; both are named and located so a later round can go and get them.

variants.label: MODERN PRACTITIONER convention — 真太陽時 (true solar time) correction
variants.authority: Modern bazi practice, Tier C. Contested within that practice.
variants.arithmetic: Rather than reading the shichen off the civil clock, the practitioner converts the civil time to local apparent solar time — applying (a) a longitude correction against the standard meridian of the time zone (4 min per degree) and (b) the equation of time — and reads the shichen off THAT. The argument for it is that the classical water clock was set to local 夜半/日中 and so was local apparent time by construction, making the correction a restoration rather than an innovation. The argument against is that the classical texts state no such correction and the 96-ke Qing reckoning was itself a civil standard. BOTH POSITIONS ARE HELD BY LIVING PRACTITIONERS AND NEITHER IS ADOPTED HERE.
variants.note: STRUCTURALLY IMPORTANT: this variant is the ONLY thing that makes shichen location-dependent. Without it, shichen boundaries are identical in Beijing, Ürümqi and Hong Kong — which is exactly the objection the true-solar-time party raises, since Ürümqi and Beijing share UTC+8 while sitting ~30° of longitude apart, roughly two hours of apparent time.

variants.label: MODERN PRACTITIONER dispute — 早子時 / 晚子時 (夜子時) and where the day changes
variants.authority: Live dispute in modern bazi practice, Tier C on both sides
variants.arithmetic: Position 1 (子時換日, reported as mainstream): 23:00–01:00 is one 子 hour and the DAY-pillar changes at 23:00, so a birth at 23:30 on the 5th already carries the 6th's day stem-branch. Position 2 (早/晚子時, attributed to 袁樹珊 Yuan Shushan and reported as the minority): the day changes at 00:00 (子正); 23:00–24:00 is 晚子時/夜子時 and keeps the current day's stem-branch while taking the 子 branch for the hour. The two give different day pillars for anyone born in that one hour. The Tier C sources report that classical divinatory texts contain no worked example of Position 2 — I have NOT verified that negative claim.

variants.label: PREDECESSOR scheme — the fifteen solar stations of 淮南子·天文訓
variants.authority: 淮南子 (c. 139 BCE), 天文訓
variants.arithmetic: NOT twelve. The Huainanzi tracks the sun through named places and gives FIFTEEN named time-divisions: 晨明・朏明・旦明・蚤食・晏食・隅中・正中・小還・𫗦時・大還・高舂・下舂・縣車・黃昏・定昏. Two of these (隅中, 黃昏) survive into the later twelve-name Han set; the rest do not. This is a genuinely different division of the day and is recorded so that nobody reads the twelve-name set back into the Western Han.
variants.note: NO SCHOLAR IS CITED HERE deriving the twelve from the fifteen, or the reverse. The two schemes are printed side by side and no direction of development is asserted.

variants.label: The twelve animals — what is actually attested, and where
variants.authority: 論衡 (王充, c. 80 CE), chapters 物勢 and 言毒
variants.arithmetic: n/a — an attestation claim, not a computation
variants.note: TWO SEPARATE CLAIMS, kept separate. (1) VERIFIED: 論衡 物勢篇 gives eleven branch–animal pairs and is SILENT on 辰; 論衡 言毒篇 supplies 辰為龍. The complete twelve therefore exist in 論衡 only as a reconstruction across two chapters. (2) NOT VERIFIED, AND ATTRIBUTED, NOT ASSERTED: tertiary sources report that the Shuihudi 睡虎地 Qin daybook (日書, c. 217 BCE) and the Fangmatan 放馬灘 slips carry an earlier and PARTLY DIFFERENT animal–branch scheme, and that 論衡 is the earliest extant text with the modern set. I did not reach a primary or peer-reviewed statement of either claim, and this dossier makes no priority claim of its own.

polarBehaviour: THE SHICHEN LAYER HAS NO POLAR FAILURE MODE, and that is a structural fact worth stating loudly in a comparison view. Because the twelve divisions are defined by clock time and not by any solar event, they are total functions of the civil timestamp: they are as well defined at Longyearbyen on 21 December as at the equator, and they are identical at both. Nothing degrades, nothing returns null, no fallback is needed. Contrast the two systems already in this repo: planetary-hours.js returns null when SearchRiseSet finds no sunrise or sunset, and any sunrise-anchored muhūrta scheme has the same problem. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE COMPARISON PAGE: the honest reading is not 'shichen are more robust'. It is that shichen ANSWER A DIFFERENT QUESTION — they are a civil calendar-of-the-day, not an observation of the sky — and a page that presents robustness as a virtue is comparing a clock to a sundial and awarding points. THE ADJACENT LAYERS DO DEGRADE, and must be flagged separately: (a) the 更 night-watches run dusk→dawn and are undefined wherever civil twilight does not occur, i.e. above roughly the Arctic and Antarctic circles in the relevant seasons; (b) the 隋書 daylight/darkness ke split (冬至 40/60 etc.) is a table computed for one standard latitude — Sôma et al. (2004) find the Chinese tables correspond to about 34.5°N — and is simply wrong elsewhere, not adjustable; (c) the modern 真太陽時 practitioner correction does NOT fail at the poles (the sun's hour angle is defined everywhere) but becomes meaningless as a civil convenience there.

gaps: DAY STEM-BRANCH (日干支) — THE BIGGEST GAP, AND IT BLOCKS TWO LAYERS. Both the 五鼠遁 hour-stem rule and the 協紀辨方書 hour-spirit rule need the DAY's stem-branch, and this dossier does not supply a published, fetchable table mapping a Gregorian date to one. I checked the obvious official routes and they do not carry it: the Hong Kong Observatory's Gregorian–Lunar conversion tables (English and Chinese, 2026) give lunar date, weekday and solar term only, with the year's 干支 in the title and nothing per-day; Taiwan's 中央氣象署 astronomy download page lists sunrise/sunset, moonrise/moonset, star charts and solar-term dates, with no 日干支 product linked. The named scholarly authorities — 陳垣《二十史朔閏表》(1926, PD in the US) and 張培瑜《三千五百年曆日天象》 — I did not obtain. CONSEQUENCE: gv-3, gv-4 and gv-7 are deliberately keyed to a stem-branch (甲子日, 乙丑日, 甲 day) rather than to a calendar date, so that the hour layer can be tested WITHOUT this gap being closed first. Phase 2 must not paper over it by generating day-ganzhi from an unsourced formula.

THE MERIDIAN / ORGAN COLUMN IS UNVERIFIED AT PRIMARY LEVEL. Every organ association in entries[] rests on zhenjiu-dacheng-nazhi, whose primary transcription failed to fetch (expired TLS certificate on zysj.com.cn) and whose locus (針灸大成 卷五) reached me only through secondary pages. The earlier attribution to 《子午流注針經》 (1153) is equally unverified. This column should either be verified against a printed 針灸大成 or dropped. It should NOT ship at the same visual weight as the 論衡 and 五行大義 columns.

THE CLASSICAL TWELVE NAMES (夜半・雞鳴・平旦…) have no verified primary locus here. The standard attribution is to 杜預's commentary on the 左傳; zh-wiki-shichen cites it and I did not reach the commentary itself. The names are carried at Tier C for their attribution even though they are uncontroversial in substance.
五鼠遁's attribution to 《淵海子平》 is unverified — the Chinese Wikisource transcription is explicitly incomplete (此文檔未完成) and lacks the passage. The arithmetic is certain; the locus is not.

THE 120-KE EPISODE (Wang Mang / Xin) has no primary locus here. 隋書 卷19 gives me 507, 544 and the Chen restoration; it did not yield the 120-ke episode in the section I read. en-wiki-tct confirms that 96-, 108- and 120-ke days existed for short periods but supplies no dates. The Wang Mang attribution is tertiary only.

THE 元武/玄武 SPELLING in the 四庫全書 協紀辨方書 is recorded as printed, but I could NOT verify the usual explanation (Qing avoidance of 玄, the Kangxi Emperor's name 玄燁). What I did find is an unrelated Song precedent (真宗 avoiding 玄 → 真武). The taboo explanation is therefore NOT asserted.

THE 庚午日 ROW of 協紀辨方書 卷32 did not extract cleanly — the retrieval returned three spirits in one cell and a bare fragment in another, plainly a table-alignment artefact. Its anchor cells (子=金匱, 申=青龍, 酉=明堂, 戌=天刑, 亥=朱雀) do agree with the closed form, but the row is NOT offered as a golden value. Only the two rows that came back clean and complete are. A third row should be read off a page image before the rule is called fully validated.

SÔMA ET AL. (2004) WAS NOT READ IN FULL. The Song 0h-start finding, the varying fen-per-ke finding and the 34.5°N standard-latitude finding all come from journal-page summary content, not from pp. 887–904. No page numbers can be given for them, and anyone relying on the Song variant should obtain the article.

NO LATITUDE IS ATTACHED TO THE 隋書 40/60 SOLSTICE SPLIT by the source itself. The arithmetic (60 ke × 14.4 min = 14.4 h of midsummer daylight) is the source's own numbers, but the inference to a latitude is not made in 隋書, and I have deliberately not made it. Sôma et al.'s 34.5°N finding is adjacent but I have not verified that the 40/60 figure is among the data they analysed.

NO SCHOLAR IS CITED connecting the fifteen solar stations of 淮南子·天文訓 to the twelve-branch scheme in either direction. Both are printed; no development is asserted. Under the project's no-original-diffusion rule, there is no row until someone has published the comparison.

THE SHUIHUDI / FANGMATAN PRIORITY CLAIM about the twelve animals is tertiary only. That the Qin daybooks carry an earlier and partly different animal-branch scheme, and that 論衡 is the earliest extant witness to the modern set, are both REPORTED here as claims of others and neither is verified against a primary publication or a peer-reviewed study.

NO PUBLISHED TONG SHU PAGE FOR A NAMED CALENDAR DATE was obtained. The 協紀辨方書 table is keyed to the sexagenary day, which is better for testing, but it means this dossier carries no fixture of the form 'the almanac for such-and-such a printed year marks these hours auspicious on this date'. That would be the ideal end-to-end fixture and it is missing.
contestedPoints: WHERE 子 BEGINS. Mainstream and near-universal: 子 straddles midnight, 23:00–01:00, and the branch's own name 夜半 presupposes it. Against: Sôma, Kawabata & Tanikawa (2004) find the Song dynasty began the first double-hour at 0h local time, giving 子 = 00:00–02:00 and shifting every division. A human must rule on whether the comparison page offers the Song reckoning as a selectable convention or footnotes it. It is not a rounding difference — it relabels every hour of the day.

WHEN THE 96-KE REFORM ACTUALLY TOOK. Three dated positions, all printed here: 1628 (en-wiki-tct dates the redefinition to the 崇禎曆書 project); 1645 (zh-wiki-ke, lin-2007 and most sources: promulgation of the 時憲曆 in 順治二年); and not-until-1668/69 (清史稿 卷45 shows the 100-vs-96 question still being argued at court in 康熙四年 = 1665 and settled only after the Verbiest observatory trial). A human must decide which the engine's pre/post-reform toggle uses, and the page must name whose date it is.

WHETHER THE 96-KE SYSTEM IS A EUROPEAN IMPORT. It is universally told that way, and the Jesuit role in 1645 is real. But 隋書 records the identical reform, for the identical arithmetical reason, in Liang 天監 6 (507 CE) — eleven centuries earlier. Whether that makes the Qing reform a re-adoption or an independent import is a real scholarly question and no cited scholar here answers it. The site must not answer it either.

THE 早子時 / 晚子時 DAY-CHANGE. Living dispute among practising bazi astrologers. Position 1 (reported mainstream): the day-pillar changes at 23:00. Position 2 (attributed to 袁樹珊, reported minority): it changes at 00:00, and 23:00–24:00 is 夜子時, taking the 子 branch but the current day's pillar. Anyone born in that one hour gets a different chart. Both positions cite classical authority against the other. A human must decide whether the engine defaults to one, offers both, or refuses to pick — and this is a living tradition, so the wrong default is a substantive editorial claim, not a UX choice.

TRUE SOLAR TIME. Whether the shichen should be read off the civil clock or off local apparent time is disputed within current practice. The stake is concrete: Ürümqi and Beijing share UTC+8 across roughly 30° of longitude, about two hours of apparent time, so the two conventions put a Ürümqi birth two shichen apart. The classical texts state no correction; the classical clepsydra was nonetheless set locally. Both readings are defensible and this dossier adopts neither.
THE READING OF 昳 IN 日昳. Given as dié in Chinese reference works, transliterated Rìyì by en-wiki-tct. A transliteration column has to choose. Someone should.

天德 vs 寶光 AS THE SIXTH SPIRIT. The 四庫全書 協紀辨方書 prints 寶光; most modern lists give 天德, and practitioner sources treat 寶光 as an alternate name for the same 黃道 spirit. Whether these are one spirit under two names or a recension difference is not established here.

WHETHER THE ALMANAC LAYER BELONGS IN THE SAME TABLE AS THE COSMOLOGY. 隋書, 論衡 and 五行大義 give the divisions, the animals and the phases and assign NO RULER TO ANY HOUR. Rulership enters only through the almanac, keyed to the day. Presenting a 'ruler' column beside the planetary-hours ruler column risks manufacturing a parallel the Chinese sources do not make. The brief asked for the Tong Shu layer clearly labelled as almanac-derived; this dossier does that, but a human should rule on whether it may share a column header with a system that genuinely has hour-lords.
honestLimits: This system tells you what the sources say a two-hour slice of the day is called, what animal and which of the five phases the tradition attaches to it, and — from an eighteenth-century imperial almanac, and only from there — which of twelve spirits sits on that hour of that day. That is the whole of it, and none of it is a claim about what will happen. The twelve shichen are a naming convention for clock time. They are not an observation: 卯 is called 'sunrise' and runs 05:00 to 07:00 whether or not the sun rises, which at most latitudes it usually does not. Anything this page can compute about them is arithmetic on a timestamp, and arithmetic on a timestamp is checkable, which is the only reason it is here. What is NOT checkable is every association hanging off it. The animal, the phase, the direction and the almanac spirit are what named texts assign, reported in those texts' voice, and the site has no view on whether any of it corresponds to anything. The auspicious-hour layer in particular is a printed table, and reproducing a printed table is evidence about eighteenth-century Chinese almanac practice and about nothing else — the site does not suggest choosing an hour by it, and there is no affordance here for doing so. The organ column is weaker still: it is an unverified attribution to a 1601 acupuncture compendium, it is recorded because the tradition records it, and it is not health information in any sense. Nobody should read a claim about their body out of it. Three further limits the page must carry in its own voice rather than in a footnote. First, the numbers here are location-blind by construction: unlike every other system on this page, shichen do not know where you are, and if you want them to, you have entered a live disagreement among practitioners that this site does not settle. Second, the boundaries the page draws are a modern civil mapping; the classical instrument was a water clock set locally, and the 100-ke reckoning it used does not align with the 96-ke boundaries shown, so a Tang date and a Qing date are not being read on the same dial. Third, this is a living tradition — the almanac is in print and in daily use — and the arguments recorded here about where the day changes are current arguments among people who practise, not curiosities from a closed corpus. They are set out because they are unresolved, not because the site has resolved them.
